analysis.one_liner: Bans open-market stock buybacks and requires employee-elected directors on a third of public company boards.
analysis.headline: The Reward Work Act, a bill to ban open-market stock buybacks and give workers a third of the seats on corporate boards, died in a House committee without a vote after two Democrats introduced it with 13 cosponsors and no Senate action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop publicly traded companies from buying back their own shares on the open market — a practice companies used to boost their stock prices, which raises the value of executive stock pay. It would also require that one-third of a public company's board of directors be elected by its own employees, one employee one vote, so workers have a direct seat at the table where executive pay and corporate priorities are set. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any movement before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of publicly traded companies would gain worker-elected seats on corporate boards, giving them a voice in decisions like pay, buybacks, and layoffs. Proponents argue workers would also gain indirectly if money that now goes to buybacks were redirected to wages or productive investment. Ordinary retirement savers could see steadier corporate capital use instead of price-boosting repurchases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public company employees and workers broadly

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits any issuer from purchasing its own equity securities on a registered national securities exchange, and voids the SEC safe-harbor rule (Rule 10b-18) that currently shields routine buyback programs from manipulation liability.

It amends the Securities Exchange Act so no issuer may register securities on a national exchange unless at least one-third of its directors are chosen by employees in a one-employee-one-vote election, with SEC and NLRB rules required to make those elections fair and in place within two years.
Under the bill, workers would hold a guaranteed bloc of board seats, changing the audience executives answer to when deciding how corporate profits are spent.
The bill preserves genuine tender offers (a different, regulated way of repurchasing shares directly from shareholders), so the buyback prohibition is targeted at open-market repurchases.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies and their executives would pay first: buyback programs are a standard way to lift stock prices, which drive executive pay packages. Large institutional shareholders who rely on buyback-driven price appreciation would forgo that channel of returns, and investment banks and trading firms that earn fees executing buyback programs would lose business. Some defenders of buybacks argue consumers and pension holders ultimately bear costs if companies lose a flexible way to return capital.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives, large shareholders, and buyback-fee earners

drawbacks.text: Buybacks are a lawful, common way to return excess cash to shareholders, and defenders argue they recycle capital to more productive uses; an outright ban would leave dividends as the main alternative, which carries different tax treatment and less flexibility for companies.

A blanket prohibition on open-market repurchases eliminates the anti-manipulation guardrails of Rule 10b-18's replacement framework entirely rather than conditioning buybacks, so companies with legitimate reasons to repurchase shares would have no compliant path outside tender offers.

Mandating one-third employee-elected directors is a sweeping federal intervention in corporate governance; it resembles German co-determination, which critics say can slow board decisions and raise friction between employee directors and shareholder-elected directors, and its benefits for wages are indirect and not guaranteed.
Critics argue buybacks are not the driver of low wages some claim, and that banning them could reduce returns for 401(k) and pension investors who are themselves ordinary savers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to workers are real but partly indirect: the board-seat requirement gives employees genuine governance power, while the buyback ban's benefit to workers depends on companies choosing to redirect freed-up cash to wages and investment rather than dividends. The costs fall on executives, large shareholders, and buyback fee-earners — which is precisely the point of the bill — but ordinary 401(k) investors could also see some return-channel effects. The buyback ban is blunt; a per-transaction fee or a wage-linked condition would have been less of a sledgehammer. On balance, the bill targets a practice that concentrated executives' benefit from corporate profits, and its board mandate is a structural change whose effects would have taken years to know.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia introduced the Reward Work Act in the House on October 7, 2022, with 13 Democratic cosponsors, less than three months before that Congress ended.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on October 7, 2022, and no further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
All 13 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Senate version or Senate action appears in the record for this bill.

Buybacks had reached record levels in the years before the bill, which sponsors framed as profits enriching executives and shareholders rather than workers — an argument reflected in the bill's title, the 'Reward Work Act'.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate executives and large shareholders, whose companies remain free to repurchase their own shares, and the investment banks that earn fees running buyback programs — plus the House Financial Services Committee, whose inaction preserved the status quo without anyone having to vote against the bill on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives, large shareholders, and buyback fee-earners

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Reward Work Act in the House on October 7, 2022.

for.name: 13 of 221 House Democrats (at introduction)
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. DeFazio, Khanna, Ocasio-Cortez, Jayapal, and Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no cosponsors from any other party.

against.name: Chair Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on October 7, 2022 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Held the majority and floor schedule; never brought the bill to the floor, and no Republican supported it in committee or on the record.

against.name: Financial industry and corporate lobby groups
against.what_they_did: The broader business and financial sector strongly opposed mandatory worker board representation and buyback restrictions as a class of proposals during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat — Garcia plus 13 Democratic cosponsors — and no Republican supported it; with a Democratic committee chair declining to act and Republican control of the chamber's agenda, the bill faced opposition on both sides of the aisle, in different ways.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: The bill would end open-market buybacks that lift stock prices — the basis of much executive pay — and put employee-elected directors on boards, cutting into management's sole control of profit allocation. Executives and managers were the bill's clearest losers, which is why corporate interests opposed proposals like it.

industries.industry: Investment banks, broker-dealers, and trading firms
industries.note: Banks and trading firms earn fees and volume executing buyback programs; a ban on open-market repurchases removes that business line. Their interest in keeping buybacks runs against workers' interest in seeing profits spent elsewhere.

Large shareholders benefit from buyback-driven price gains and would lose that channel, but they would also lose flexibility to have companies return capital. Some asset managers supported co-determination-style board reform; others opposed it. The effect is genuinely two-sided here.
Not an industry, but the bill's direct beneficiary class: workers would elect one-third of their company's board and gain a structural voice in pay and capital decisions.
